unit.title: Basic Concepts, Pure Substances and the First Law (Closed Systems)

content.back: An axiomatic science which deals with the relations among heat, work and properties of a system which are in equilibrium. It describes state and changes in state of physical systems.

cards.why: This is the opening definition in your own notes and the standard one-mark opener.

content.prompt: Name the four laws of thermodynamics and state what each one establishes.
items: Zeroth law — deals with thermal equilibrium and establishes the concept of temperature
First law — throws light on the concept of internal energy
Second law — indicates the limit of converting heat into work and introduces the principle of increase in entropy
Third law — defines the absolute zero of entropy

cards.trap: The zeroth law is numbered last historically but comes first logically — it is what makes temperature measurable at all.

content.back:
System — a finite quantity of matter or a prescribed region of space.
Boundary — the actual or hypothetical envelope enclosing the system. It may be fixed or it may move, as when a system containing a gas is compressed or extended. It may be real or imaginary.
Surroundings — the mass or region outside the system.

cards.trap: A boundary is allowed to move and is allowed to be imaginary. Both facts are examinable and both get forgotten.

content.prompt: Name the three system types classified by what crosses the boundary, and state what crosses in each.
items: Closed system (control mass) — energy crosses, mass does not
Open system (control volume) — both mass and energy cross
Isolated system — neither mass nor energy crosses

cards.why: Choosing the system type is the first line of every numerical you will write. Get it wrong and every equation after it is the wrong equation.

content.front: What is an open system, and why are most engineering problems modelled as one?
content.back: An open system, or control volume, is a properly selected region in space. It usually encloses a device that involves mass flow such as a compressor, turbine or nozzle. A large number of engineering problems involve mass flow in and out of the system and are therefore modelled as control volumes.

cards.trap: Most control volumes have fixed boundaries and so involve no moving-boundary work — but a control volume can also involve heat and work interactions just like a closed system, in addition to mass interaction.

content.front: Distinguish a homogeneous system from a heterogeneous system, with an example of each.
content.back:
A homogeneous system consists of a single phase — e.g. a mixture of air and water vapour, or octane plus heptane.
A heterogeneous system consists of two or more phases — e.g. water plus nitric acid.

content.front: Contrast the macroscopic and microscopic approaches to thermodynamics.
content.back:
Macroscopic — a certain quantity of matter is considered without taking into account the events occurring at molecular level. This is classical thermodynamics. Analysis requires simple mathematical formulae, and property values are their average values: pressure and temperature can be measured easily.
Microscopic — the system is made up of a very large number of discrete particles which have different velocities and energies changing constantly with time. This is statistical. Behaviour is found by statistical methods and advanced mathematics is needed; properties like velocity, momentum and KE cannot be felt.

cards.why: Classic 5-mark 'differentiate' question, and your notes give it as a two-column table — reproduce it as a table in the exam.

content.text: Properties that do not depend on the mass of the system are called {{intensive}} properties, for example {{temperature and pressure}}. Properties that do depend on mass are called {{extensive}} properties, for example {{volume}}.

cards.trap: Extensive properties per unit mass become specific properties, and a specific property is intensive: specific volume v = V/m, specific total energy e = E/m.

content.prompt: State 1 atm in Pa and in bar, and state 1 bar in Pa.

cards.trap: 1 bar is not 1 atm. The 1.3 % difference is enough to lose a mark in a manometer problem.

content.prompt: State the ideal gas equation in mass form and define every symbol with its unit.
content.note: Also written Pv = RT per unit mass, where v is specific volume.

symbols.means: specific gas constant (287 J/kg·K for air)

cards.trap: T must be absolute (K) and P must be absolute, never gauge. R here is the specific gas constant, not the universal one — 287 J/kg·K is air only.

content.prompt: State the relation between Cp, Cv and R, and give the values used in your class test.
content.note: Class test instruction: take Cp = 1.005 kJ/kg·K and Cv = 0.717 kJ/kg·K for air. These give R = 0.288 kJ/kg·K ≈ 287 J/kg·K.

cards.why: These two numbers are printed on your class test paper as a standing instruction — they are given to you, but knowing them means you can check your own arithmetic.
cards.source: Own notes p.14; Class Test 1 instructions, 4/8/2026

content.front: Why do real gases deviate from ideal gas behaviour? Give both reasons.
content.back:
1. Intermolecular forces exist. In reality gas molecules attract and repel each other; at low temperatures attractive forces such as van der Waals forces become significant.
2. Molecular volume is not negligible. An ideal gas ignores the volume of the individual molecules, but at high pressure the particles are close together so their finite size matters.

cards.trap: The two reasons map onto the two correction terms in van der Waals: a/v² corrects for attraction, b corrects for volume.

content.prompt: State the van der Waals equation of state and define its constants.

symbols.means: van der Waals constants, converted per kg

cards.trap: a and b are usually tabulated on a molar basis. Your notes flag 'converted per kg' — if you use molar constants with specific volume the answer is out by the molar mass squared.

content.front: Define a pure substance and state whether it can exist in more than one phase.
content.back: A substance that has a fixed chemical composition throughout is called a pure substance — such as water, air and nitrogen. A pure substance may exist in different phases: solid, liquid and gas.

cards.trap: A mixture can still be a pure substance as long as its composition is uniform — air counts. But a mixture of liquid air and gaseous air does not, because the phases have different compositions.

content.prompt: Name the three latent heats and state the phase change each corresponds to.
items: Latent heat of vaporisation — liquid to gas, without a change in temperature
Latent heat of sublimation — solid directly to gas
Latent heat of fusion — solid to liquid, without any change in temperature

cards.trap: Latent heat moves no temperature. If your solution shows a ΔT during a phase change, the phase change is where the error is.

content.front: Define the triple point and the critical point.
content.back:
Triple point — the point at which the three phases, solid, liquid and gas, coexist.
Critical point — the point at which the pure substance does not require latent heat for phase transformation.

cards.why: Both are labelled points on the P–T diagram you have to draw, so the definition and the sketch are marked together.

content.front: Define saturation temperature and saturation pressure, and state their relationship during a phase change.
content.back: At a given pressure, the temperature at which a pure substance starts boiling is called the saturation temperature (T_sat). At a given temperature, the pressure at which a pure substance starts boiling is called the saturation pressure (P_sat). During a phase-change process, pressure and temperature are dependent properties.

cards.trap: Outside the dome P and T are independent and you need both to fix the state. Inside the dome they are not, which is exactly why you need quality x as the second property.

content.prompt: A pure substance at constant pressure is heated from solid to superheated vapour. Name the five states it passes through, in order.
items: Solid
Mixed phase of liquid and solid
Sub-cooled or compressed liquid (about to vaporise)
Wet vapour or saturated liquid–vapour mixture — temperature stops rising until the liquid is completely vaporised
Superheated vapour (vapour about to condense on cooling)

cards.why: This sequence is the spine of every T–v diagram question and every steam table lookup.

content.back:
The amount of vapour substance present in the system, expressed as
x = (amount of vapour) / (total mass of substance) = m_g / (m_f + m_g)

cards.trap: Quality is only defined inside the vapour dome, 0 ≤ x ≤ 1. Quoting an x for compressed liquid or superheated vapour is meaningless.

content.prompt: State the three mixture property equations for a saturated liquid–vapour mixture of quality x.
content.latex: v = v_f + x\,v_{fg} \qquad h = h_f + x\,h_{fg} \qquad s = s_f + x\,s_{fg}
content.note: v_fg = v_g − v_f, and likewise for h and s.

symbols.means: specific volume of saturated liquid, saturated vapour
enthalpy of saturated liquid, enthalpy of vaporisation

cards.why: Class Test 1 question 3 was exactly this — find the quality and the density of a saturated mixture in a rigid tank.
cards.trap: v_fg is v_g − v_f, not v_g. Substituting v_g is the single most common slip in this calculation.
cards.source: Own notes p.6; Class Test 1 Q3

content.front: Distinguish sensible heat from latent heat.
content.back:
Sensible heat is the heat energy absorbed or released that changes a substance's temperature without changing its phase — for example heating water. It can be measured with a thermometer and felt as a temperature change.
Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a phase change at constant temperature — ice to water, or boiling water to steam.

content.front: Sketch the T–v diagram of a pure substance. Label the vapour dome, the critical point, and the three regions.
content.back: Dome with saturated liquid line on the left and saturated vapour line on the right, meeting at the critical point. Compressed liquid region to the left of the dome, liquid+vapour region inside it, superheated vapour region to the right. Constant-pressure lines run through, with P increasing upward.

cards.why: The class test instructions say 'Draw the P–V diagram wherever necessary' — this is a drawing you will be marked on, not just a concept.
cards.figure_ref: Own notes p.6, right-hand page — 'VAPOR DOME', both T–v and P–v drawn side by side. Google image search: 'T-v diagram pure substance vapor dome critical point'. Label in this order: saturated liquid line, saturated vapour line, critical point, then the three regions, then one constant-pressure line.

content.back:
State — the condition of the system at an instant of time as described or measured by its properties. Each unique condition of a system is called a state.
Process — occurs when the system undergoes a change in state or an energy transfer at a steady state.
Cycle — any process or series of processes whose end states are identical.

cards.trap: Because a cycle returns to its start, every property change over a complete cycle is zero: ΔU = 0, so Q_net = W_net. That single consequence is what most cycle questions test.

content.front: What is a quasi-static process, and what is its characteristic feature?
content.back: Quasi means 'almost'. A quasi-static process is also called a reversible process. It is a succession of equilibrium states, and infinite slowness is its characteristic feature.

cards.trap: Only a quasi-static process can be drawn as a continuous line on a P–V diagram, because only then does the system have a defined pressure throughout. A non-equilibrium process gets a dashed line between two points and nothing in between.

content.front: Distinguish a point function from a path function, with examples.
content.back: When two properties locate a point on a graph, those properties are called a point function — pressure, temperature, volume. There are certain quantities that cannot be located on a graph by a point but are given by the area under the curve — these are path functions, such as work and heat.

cards.trap: This is why we write dV but δW. A property has an exact differential; work and heat do not.

content.prompt: Derive and state the boundary work of a closed system.
content.latex: \delta W = F\,ds = P A\,ds = P\,dV \quad\Rightarrow\quad W = \int_1^2 P\,dV

cards.trap: Valid only for a quasi-static process — otherwise P is not defined throughout the system and the integral has no meaning.

content.prompt: For the polytropic relation PVⁿ = constant, state the value of n for each of the four standard processes.
items: n = 0 — isobaric (constant pressure)
n = 1 — isothermal (constant temperature)
n = γ — adiabatic (isentropic)
n = ∞ — isochoric (constant volume)

cards.why: One diagram in your notes carries all four. Knowing the ladder means you can derive any of the work expressions from the polytropic one instead of memorising four.

content.prompt: State the work done in a reversible isothermal process for an ideal gas.
content.note: Since ΔU = 0 for an isothermal ideal gas process, Q = W.

cards.trap: Only for an ideal gas. And the ratio is V₂/V₁ — inverting it flips the sign and turns a compression into an expansion.

content.prompt: State the work done in a polytropic process and in a reversible adiabatic process.
content.note: The adiabatic case is the polytropic case with n = γ. For the adiabatic process Q = 0, so W = −ΔU.

symbols.means: ratio of specific heats, Cp/Cv (1.4 for air)

cards.trap: Numerator is P₁V₁ − P₂V₂, not the other way round. Writing it reversed gives the right magnitude and the wrong sign, which in a work question costs the whole mark.

content.front: Define internal energy and state what kind of property it is.
content.back: Internal energy is the total energy contained in the system, represented as the sum of the kinetic and potential energies of the particles (atoms, molecules). It is an extensive property and a point function. U is total internal energy in kJ; u is specific internal energy in kJ/kg.

content.prompt: Define enthalpy and give its ideal-gas change.
content.latex: H = U + PV \qquad h = u + Pv \qquad \Delta H = m C_p (T_2 - T_1)
content.note: Enthalpy is a measure of the total heat content of the system. It is a state function: its value depends only on the current state, not on the path taken to reach that state.

cards.trap: ΔH = mCpΔT holds for an ideal gas in any process, not only a constant-pressure one. The same goes for ΔU = mCvΔT.

content.prompt: State the first-law results (Q, ΔU, W) for the five standard closed-system processes of an ideal gas.
items: Isochoric (V const): W = 0, ΔU = mCv(T₂−T₁), Q = ΔU = mCv(T₂−T₁)
Isobaric (P const): W = P(V₂−V₁), ΔU = mCv(T₂−T₁), Q = ΔH = mCp(T₂−T₁)
Isothermal (T const): ΔU = 0, W = mRT ln(V₂/V₁), Q = W
Polytropic (PVⁿ = c): W = (P₁V₁−P₂V₂)/(n−1), ΔU = mCv(T₂−T₁), Q = ΔU + W
Adiabatic (PVᵞ = c): Q = 0, W = (P₁V₁−P₂V₂)/(γ−1) = −ΔU

cards.why: This is the single table your notes build the whole of the first law towards. If you can reproduce these five rows cold, most of a first-law numerical is already done.
cards.trap: Your notes' summary box compresses the isobaric row to 'Q = ΔU'; that is shorthand for the derivation, not the result. For isobaric, Q equals ΔH, not ΔU.
cards.source: Own notes p.16 (first-law analysis table and summary box)

content.front: State the first law for a cyclic process and the consequence for net heat and net work.
content.back: Over a complete cycle the system returns to its initial state, so every property change is zero — in particular ΔU = 0. The first law Q = ΔU + W therefore reduces to Q_net = W_net: the net heat transfer over a cycle equals the net work done.

cards.why: Practice question 2 on the First Law sheet is exactly this — four heat transfers given, find the net work — and it is a one-line answer if you know this.

content.text: By the sign convention used throughout the course, heat supplied to the system is {{positive}}, heat rejected by the system is {{negative}}, work done by the system is {{positive}}, and work done on the system is {{negative}}.

cards.trap: Every 'determine the direction and magnitude' question is really a sign-convention question. Class Test Q1 and practice questions 1, 7 and 8 all hinge on it.
cards.source: First Law practice questions, 24/7/26, Q1 and Q7

content.prompt: For water at atmospheric pressure, what value of specific heat does your course use, and in which equation?
content.value: Cp for water = 4.187 kJ/kg·K, used in Q = m·C·ΔT
content.context: c is the specific heat at constant pressure; m is mass.
